narrativeReportMd:
# Consent R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R6 keeps the `Consent` resource identity but substantially remodels its local content. There are multiple hard R4-to-R6 validation breaks: required `scope` is removed, several old elements are renamed or replaced, policy fields are restructured, `status` required codes change, and provision permit/deny semantics move to a new modifier element.

## Scope
This analysis covers local `Consent` StructureDefinition changes and related local terminology. It excludes inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element/BackboneElement changes, search parameters, profiles, and server behavior.

## Main migration themes
The dominant migration theme is semantic remodelling rather than small cardinality tweaks. R4 Consent encoded scope, patient, performer, organization, dateTime, policy/policyRule, source choice, provision type, and broad provision class fields. R6 replaces many of these with subject, grantor/grantee, manager/controller, date/period, regulatoryBasis/policyBasis/policyText, separate source arrays, root decision, documentType/resourceType, and optional expression.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-risk changes are removal of required `scope`, the required `status` code-set change, the policy/policyRule replacement and invariant removal, the participant-role remodel, and the permit/deny move from `provision.type` to modifier `Consent.decision`. These can invalidate old data and can change consent enforcement if migrated incorrectly.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is especially important for mapping `scope`, `performer`, `organization`, `policyRule`, `provision.type`, and `provision.class`, because the same R4 content may map to different R6 elements depending on local consent policy semantics.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Many R6 changes look semantically motivated, but several could have been staged less disruptively by retaining deprecated R4 elements or publishing explicit cross-version ConceptMaps. R6-to-R4 downgrade is also materially lossy when R6 uses non-patient subjects, multiple source items, manager/controller fields, policyBasis/policyText, multiple provisions, or provision expressions.

## Follow-up analysis
A complete migration plan should include terminology-server-backed expansion comparison, official ballot diffs/change proposals, search parameter migration, and base Resource/DomainResource change reports.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: R6 `Consent` is the same artifact identity but has substantial local breaking changes. Top concerns are mandatory R4 `scope` removal, required `status` vocabulary changes, policy/provision remodels, and ambiguous actor/policy/content-class migrations. The main uncertainty is lack of official cross-version mappings and narrative rationale.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should be treated as a domain transform, not a field rename. Several R4 elements were overloaded (`performer`, `policyRule`, `provision.class`) and need local interpretation before mapping. R6 adds more expressive constructs (`subject`, `grantor`/`grantee`, `decision`, `policyBasis`, `provision.expression`) that improve modeling but create lossy R6-to-R4 downgrade paths.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural, cardinality, type, flag, and local terminology deltas because both StructureDefinitions and key local terminology artifacts were inspected. Confidence is medium for the intended migration semantics because official diffs, ballot rationale, full narrative pages, terminology expansions, and cross-version ConceptMaps were not available in the local inputs.

findings.title: Required Consent.scope was removed and the scope/category model was loosened

oldState.summary: Consent.scope was mandatory and modifier-like: 1..1 CodeableConcept with an extensible ConsentScope binding.

binding.description: The four anticipated uses for the Consent Resource.

semanticText.short: Which of the four areas this resource covers (extensible)
semanticText.definition: A selector of the type of consent being presented: ADR, Privacy, Treatment, Research. This list is now extensible.

oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 every valid `Consent` carried `scope`, typically one of `adr`, `research`, `patient-privacy`, or `treatment`. R4 also had local `ppc-*` constraints tying some scopes to `patient`.

newState.summary: No Consent.scope element exists in R6. Consent.category remains, but is optional and example-bound.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 removes the separate scope axis. `Consent.category` changes from `1..*` extensible to `0..*` example, and its example ValueSet includes the former consent-scope code system, but that is not a direct structural replacement.

facts.note: Related local change: category is no longer mandatory.
Scope/patient-specific constraints are no longer present locally in R6.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `Consent.scope` has no same-path R6 element. The closest computable home for some scope codes is `Consent.category`, because the R6 category example ValueSet includes `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope`, but the StructureDefinition does not declare a formal rename.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct R4-to-R6 validation break because a conformant R4 instance must contain `scope`, and R6 has no `Consent.scope` element. It is also a semantic migration risk: dropping scope loses the high-level purpose of the consent unless it is intentionally remapped, commonly to `category` or jurisdiction-specific policy metadata. R6-to-R4 is risky because R6 permits no category/scope-like element at all.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Consent scope drives privacy, treatment, advance directive, and research handling. Losing or misclassifying it can change access-control or workflow behavior.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Removing mandatory `Consent.scope` is highly disruptive because essentially all conformant R4 instances carried it and it influenced consent purpose and related constraints. The R6 goal of not requiring a separate scope axis is plausible, but the local evidence does not show that full removal from the base resource was necessary. A staged legacy field would have avoided many validation failures, although the overlap with R6 category/policy modeling is material.
justification.inferredGoal: Simplify Consent by eliminating a separate required scope axis and folding categorization/policy meaning into other optional elements.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain Consent.scope as optional/deprecated, or define a formal equivalence to category/regulatoryBasis, but only with conflict rules.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep R4 `Consent.scope` as `0..1`, likely deprecated and no longer required, while adding R6 guidance or invariants mapping former scope codes to `category` or `regulatoryBasis` where applicable. That would preserve R4-valid data and allow new R6 records to omit scope. It is only a partial alternative because processors would need to reconcile scope with category/policy basis, and a stale modifier-style legacy field could persist indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances but leaves a second high-level consent classification/modifier axis that can conflict with category or policy metadata.

evidence.detail: R4 has `Consent.scope` with min 1, max 1, type CodeableConcept, isModifier true, and extensible ConsentScope binding.
No R6 element has path or id `Consent.scope`.
R4 root constraints refer to scope codes and patient presence.
R6 has no local `ppc-*` scope/patient constraints.

examples.examplesMd: The examples are illustrative fragments. A real migration must also handle the removed R4 `policyRule` element and any profile-specific category requirements.

findings.narrativeMd: `Consent.scope` is one of the highest-impact local removals because it was required in R4. Without transformation, essentially every valid R4 Consent instance will contain an element that the R6 resource no longer allows. The removal also changes conformance semantics: R6 does not require a replacement category and does not retain the R4 scope-driven patient constraints.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid instances containing `scope` are R6-invalid under strict validation. R6 instances can omit any scope/category equivalent, so they are not cleanly representable as R4 Consent, where `scope` was mandatory. Generated R4 code, search criteria, FHIRPath rules, and access-control logic that branch on `Consent.scope` need explicit redesign.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all `scope` values and define an implementation-specific mapping, most likely to `Consent.category` or a cross-version extension when a lossless mapping is required. Re-test rules that previously depended on `patient-privacy`, `research`, `adr`, or `treatment`, including cases where R4 constraints required a patient.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been staged more compatibly by keeping `scope` as deprecated/optional and adding R6 elements in parallel. The cost would have been overlap and possible disagreement between `scope` and the new model, but existing R4 instances would not all need structural rewrites.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is needed to decide whether a former scope code should become `category`, `regulatoryBasis`, a profile slice, or an extension in a particular implementation.

findings.title: Consent.status required code set changed: proposed/rejected removed and not-done/unknown added

oldState.summary: Required binding to R4 ConsentState: draft, proposed, active, rejected, inactive, entered-in-error.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: CodeSystem concepts were compared directly from the local packages; no terminology server expansion was run.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed `proposed` for negotiation-stage consents and `rejected` for consents rejected by one or more parties.

newState.summary: Required binding to R6 ConsentState: draft, active, inactive, not-done, entered-in-error, unknown.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 canonical status ConceptMap maps `not-done` to resource-status `failed`; it does not provide an R4-to-R6 ConceptMap for the removed R4 status codes.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 replaces the negotiation/rejection statuses with `not-done` and `unknown`, while keeping `draft`, `active`, `inactive`, and `entered-in-error`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Because the binding is required, `status: proposed` and `status: rejected` are old-valid/new-invalid. Conversely, R6 `not-done` and `unknown` cannot be represented using the R4 required code set without a lossy mapping or extension. Status is also a modifier element, so enum switches and consent enforcement logic often treat every value as behaviorally significant.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Consent status determines whether a consent should be enforced, ignored, or treated as incomplete.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Rationalizing Consent lifecycle status is a reasonable goal, and status is a modifier element with direct enforcement consequences. Keeping the removed R4 codes would preserve old instances, but it would also keep old lifecycle states whose semantics are not clean aliases for the new R6 states. Because the alternative has material safety and terminology-precision tradeoffs, the breaking required-binding change is probably justified despite needing explicit migration guidance.
justification.inferredGoal: Align Consent status with a smaller canonical resource-status lifecycle and distinguish abandoned/unknown states.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain proposed and rejected as deprecated status codes for one release, with a normative R4-to-R6 ConceptMap.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Deprecated aliases in the required ValueSet would be a real base-design alternative, not merely conversion tooling. They would allow R4 instances using `proposed` or `rejected` to validate while new implementations adopt `not-done` and `unknown`. The alternative is incomplete because mappings are context-dependent: for example, `rejected` may not mean the same thing as `not-done`, and required bindings lose precision if legacy modifier statuses remain indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves validation but weakens lifecycle rationalization and can perpetuate modifier-status values that are not equivalent to not-done or unknown.

evidence.detail: R4 binds status required to `consent-state-codes|4.0.1`.
R6 binds status required to `consent-state-codes|6.0.0-ballot4`.
R4 codes include proposed and rejected; R6 codes include not-done and unknown instead.
R6 canonical status map includes not-done -> failed and unknown -> unknown; R4 map includes proposed and rejected to resource-status but not to R6 codes.

examples.examplesMd: `rejected` might map to `not-done` for some abandoned consents, but that is not guaranteed; rejection after review may require a local status extension or audit event.

findings.narrativeMd: `Consent.status` keeps the same path and cardinality but changes the required code vocabulary. This is a hard terminology break rather than a structural rename. The removed values are not obscure lifecycle edge cases: proposed and rejected statuses are plausible in consent negotiation workflows.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A strict R6 validator must reject R4 instances using `proposed` or `rejected`. R6 instances using `not-done` or `unknown` cannot round-trip to R4 without losing the exact code. Generated enum types, switch statements, database check constraints, and UI filters need updates.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Create an explicit status migration table and review historical uses of `proposed` and `rejected`. Test enforcement behavior for active, inactive, not-done, unknown, and entered-in-error, because treating `not-done` like R4 `rejected` may be wrong for some workflows.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The code-set simplification may be justified, but it would have been less disruptive with deprecated legacy codes or a formal cross-version ConceptMap. The tradeoff is that required bindings are meant to be precise, and carrying old values can blur lifecycle semantics.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: No official R4-to-R6 status ConceptMap was found in the supplied packages.

findings.title: Consent.patient was renamed to Consent.subject and reference targets were widened

oldState.summary: Optional patient reference, 0..1, target Patient only.

semanticText.definition: The patient/healthcare consumer to whom this consent applies.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled the subject of the consent as `patient`, limited to a Patient resource.

newState.summary: Optional subject reference, 0..1, targets Patient, Practitioner, ResearchSubject, or Group.

semanticText.definition: The patient, healthcare practitioner, research subject, or a group of persons to whom this consent applies.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 generalizes the consent subject beyond patients and changes the wire element name to `subject`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The definitions and workflow mappings both identify the person or entity to whom the consent applies. The R6 element is a clear generalization of the R4 patient element.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An untransformed R4 instance with `patient` is invalid against R6 because the element no longer exists. R6 also permits non-Patient subjects that R4 cannot represent in the former `patient` slot. This impacts serializers, generated model properties, FHIRPath expressions, search parameters, and consent business rules.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misidentifying the subject of consent can change whose data or decision is governed.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Broadening Consent beyond patient-only subjects is reasonable, but the wire-path rename from `patient` to `subject` created avoidable breakage for common patient-centered R4 instances. FHIR could have tolerated the imperfect R4 name with clearer definition, broader targets, or profile guidance. If a new `subject` element was still desired, a deprecated `patient` compatibility element plus disagreement rules would have preserved old data.
justification.inferredGoal: Broaden Consent applicability beyond patient-only consents to practitioners, research subjects, and groups.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 patient element name with a broadened subject-oriented definition/target set, or keep patient as a deprecated Patient-only alias while adding subject.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `Consent.patient` as `0..1` and redefine it as the subject of consent, allowing Patient plus the new subject-like targets despite the awkward name. Another option would retain `patient` as a deprecated alias for Patient subjects and add `subject` for non-patient cases. Both preserve most or all R4 instances; the tradeoff is API terminology awkwardness and some dual-representation risk, not failure of the core R6 goal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Main cost is a nonoptimal or duplicate subject representation; that is manageable compared with forcing every patient-only instance to rename.

evidence.detail: R4 path is `Consent.patient`, targetProfile Patient.
R6 path is `Consent.subject`, targetProfile Patient, Practitioner, ResearchSubject, Group.

examples.examplesMd: Patient references migrate mechanically to `subject`; non-patient R6 subjects need an extension or cannot be represented as base R4 Consent.

findings.narrativeMd: The subject element changed from a patient-specific field to a generalized subject field. This is a predictable model improvement, but it is a wire-format break for existing instances and generated classes.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 JSON containing `patient` is not valid R6 JSON. R6 JSON containing `subject` is not valid R4 JSON, and if the subject is not a Patient there is no base R4 target to use. FHIRPath such as `Consent.patient.exists()` and search code using the R4 patient/consentor parameters must be updated.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `patient` to `subject` when the reference target is Patient. For R6-to-R4, allow only Patient subjects for lossless downgrade; otherwise use an extension or reject downgrade. Test patient, group, practitioner, and research-subject cases separately.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broader subject domain is justified by R6 use cases, but a staged alias/deprecation approach would have avoided immediate validation failure for patient-only R4 data.

findings.title: Consent.dateTime was replaced by Consent.date, narrowing precision and changing meaning

oldState.summary: Optional dateTime recording when the Consent was issued, created, or indexed.

semanticText.definition: When this Consent was issued / created / indexed.
semanticText.comment: This is not the time of the original consent, but the time that this statement was made or derived.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed time precision and described the value as the statement/indexing time, not necessarily the original agreement time.

newState.summary: Optional date recording the fully executed date/agreement date of the consent.

semanticText.definition: Date the consent instance was agreed to.
semanticText.short: Fully executed date of the consent

newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses a date-only field and changes the business meaning toward the agreement/execution date.

facts.newValue: date consent instance was agreed to

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `dateTime` fail R6 validation because the element path changed. Even after renaming, full dateTime values with a time component do not fit the R6 `date` type without truncation, and the definition no longer means exactly the same thing. R6 `date` values can usually be represented in R4 `dateTime` at date precision, but R6 also has a separate optional root `period` with no R4 equivalent.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Representing the legally executed consent date is a reasonable R6 goal, but removing and narrowing the R4 `dateTime` field was not clearly necessary. The R4 element already represented a distinct operational timestamp, and preserving it while adding an executed-date field would avoid truncation and validation failure. The less-breaking design has manageable tradeoffs.
justification.inferredGoal: Represent the executed consent date separately from effective period and avoid implying timestamp precision.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add Consent.date for executed date while retaining dateTime for legacy statement/indexing timestamp, or clarify dateTime semantics without removing it.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A compatible base design could retain `Consent.dateTime` as a deprecated legacy statement or indexing timestamp and add optional `Consent.date` for the executed agreement date. Profiles could require `date` for new records while allowing legacy `dateTime` during transition. This avoids lossy time truncation; the main cost is that implementers must distinguish agreement date from record creation/indexing time.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Two temporal fields require consistency guidance, but they preserve timestamp precision and old data with moderate model complexity.

evidence.detail: R4 element is `dateTime` with type dateTime and statement/indexing semantics.
R6 element is `date` with type date and agreement/execution semantics.
R6 also adds `Consent.period` for effective period.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example truncates the time and assumes the R4 statement time is acceptable as the R6 executed date; that assumption may be false.

findings.narrativeMd: The date field is not just renamed. The primitive type changes from `dateTime` to `date`, and the definition shifts from when the statement was made or indexed to when the consent was agreed to. Historical data may not contain the legally executed date even if it has an indexing timestamp.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Strict R6 validation rejects `dateTime` as an unknown element. If migrated to `date`, values with time-of-day must be truncated, and that transformation is lossy. Generated code changes from a dateTime property to a date property, affecting database columns, search indexes, and UI precision.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not blindly rename `dateTime` to `date`. Decide whether the R4 value represents agreement date, statement creation, or indexing. Preserve time precision in an extension, provenance record, or audit trail when needed. Add fixtures with date-only, full timestamp, timezone, and missing-date cases.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The model could have introduced a new `date` field while keeping `dateTime` deprecated. That would preserve old instances and allow implementers to move from operational timestamp to legal execution date over time.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Legal and privacy workflows may distinguish consent execution date from record creation/indexing time.

findings.title: Consent performer/custodian fields were remodeled into grantor, grantee, manager, and controller

oldState.summary: R4 used `performer` for either grantor or grantee and `organization` for the managing/custodian organization.
oldState.narrativeMd: `Consent.performer` was overloaded: its definition covered both the Grantor and the Grantee. `Consent.organization` identified the organization managing the consent.

newState.summary: R6 separates participants into `grantor`, `grantee`, `manager`, and `controller`, with widened target sets.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 has explicit grantor and grantee repeatable references, plus manager and controller roles for lifecycle management and enforcement.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `performer` text explicitly mentions Grantor and Grantee, matching the R6 `grantor` and `grantee` split. R4 `organization` is closest to R6 `manager`, but R6 also adds `controller`, so automated matching is not always deterministic.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances with `performer` or `organization` are structurally invalid in R6. Mapping `performer` requires knowing whether each actor was granting rights, agreeing to comply, or both. R6 can also express managers/controllers and new actor target types that R4 cannot represent in base fields.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Grantor/grantee/controller roles can affect who has authority to consent and who must enforce restrictions.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Disambiguating consent actors is a strong R6 goal because grantor, grantee, manager, and controller roles affect authority and enforcement. A compatibility aggregate would reduce validation breakage, but it would not recover the missing role semantics from old `performer` content and could continue the ambiguity the redesign is trying to remove. With those material tradeoffs, the split is probably justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Disambiguate consent actors and improve search/workflow roles.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain performer and organization as deprecated aggregate fields while adding explicit grantor, grantee, manager, and controller fields.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Base R6 could have accepted old `performer` and `organization` elements for a transition period while encouraging the explicit role-specific fields. That would preserve old instances, but processors would still need to classify each performer as grantor, grantee, or both, and reconcile aggregate actors with role-specific actors. Deprecated aggregate representations could persist indefinitely and create enforcement conflicts.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances but perpetuates ambiguous actor roles and duplicate or conflicting authority declarations.

evidence.detail: R4 `performer` definition says either Grantor or Grantee.
R4 `organization` identifies the custodian/managing organization.
R6 adds `grantor`.
R6 adds `grantee`.
R6 adds `manager`.
R6 adds `controller`.

examples.examplesMd: The example assumes the R4 performer was the grantor. If the same performer was actually the grantee, mapping to `grantor` would be wrong.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 replaces overloaded actor fields with role-specific fields. This improves semantics but creates a migration problem for R4 data that did not distinguish whether `performer` meant grantor or grantee.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Untransformed R4 `performer` and `organization` elements are invalid in R6. R6 `grantor`, `grantee`, `manager`, and `controller` are invalid in R4. R6 references to CareTeam, Group, or HealthcareService in grantor/grantee cannot be expressed in R4 performer without extensions because those target profiles were not allowed.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Use local business rules, profiles, or provenance to classify each R4 performer as grantor and/or grantee. Map R4 organization to R6 manager only if it really represents lifecycle management; use controller for enforcement actors. Flag ambiguous records for manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The split is probably justified because role ambiguity is dangerous for consent enforcement. A deprecated aggregate `performer` would have reduced validation breakage but prolonged ambiguity.

findings.title: Consent.source changed from a single choice element to repeatable sourceAttachment/sourceReference elements

oldState.summary: R4 `source[x]` was a 0..1 choice of Attachment or Reference.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 JSON property names were `sourceAttachment` or `sourceReference`, but they were generated from a single `source[x]` choice with an overall maximum of one.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 allows multiple attachments, multiple references, and both kinds at the same time.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Most R4 instances with a single `sourceAttachment` or single `sourceReference` use the same JSON property names in R6 and should remain structurally usable. The breaking risk is concentrated in generated models, schemas, and downgrade: R4 code often models this as one polymorphic field, while R6 models two repeatable fields and permits combinations R4 cannot carry.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing multiple source documents is a reasonable R6 goal. Simply making the old choice repeatable would not fully preserve strict R4 JSON because the cardinality change changes singleton values into arrays. A truly less-breaking base design would need to keep the old singleton choice and add new fields for additional sources, which is awkward and creates overlapping representations. The R6 split is therefore probably justified, though not completely unavoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow multiple source documents and both inline and referenced source material.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 single source[x] as a primary source and add additive source collections for additional attachments/references.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep the R4 `source[x]` singleton unchanged for a primary or legacy source and add separate additional-source arrays or a new source collection. This preserves old instances while supporting multiple sources. The tradeoff is material: processors must merge primary and additional sources, two representations for the same fact can persist indefinitely, and the model still has choice/repeatability code-generation complexity.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Would preserve old JSON but creates primary/additional source semantics and duplicate source representations; repeatable choices also burden generators.

evidence.detail: R4 has a 0..1 choice `source[x]` with Attachment or Reference.
R6 has `sourceAttachment` 0..*.
R6 has `sourceReference` 0..*.

examples.examplesMd: R4 can carry at most one source choice. The R6 example with multiple attachments plus a reference cannot be represented losslessly in base R4.

findings.narrativeMd: This is not primarily an old-valid/new-invalid break for common JSON instances, because the concrete property names overlap. It is still a material serialization and code-generation change: one polymorphic value becomes two arrays.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is usually safe for single-source instances. R6-to-R4 validation fails when more than one source is present or when both attachment and reference are present. Generated clients need API changes from a choice accessor to separate collections.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, copy `sourceAttachment` or `sourceReference` into the corresponding R6 array. For R6-to-R4, accept only zero or one total source item unless an extension or external linkage is used. Test serializers with zero, one attachment, one reference, multiple attachments, and mixed sources.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Increasing the choice cardinality would have been more conceptually compatible but may have produced less convenient generated code. The R6 split is understandable, but it requires explicit adapter code.

findings.title: Policy and policyRule were removed, replaced by regulatoryBasis/policyBasis/policyText, and the R4 policy-or-policyRule invariant disappeared

oldState.summary: R4 allowed `policy` and `policyRule`, with root invariant ppc-1 requiring at least one of them.
oldState.narrativeMd: `Consent.policy` contained authority/uri pairs and `Consent.policyRule` held a CodeableConcept for a computable regulation or policy. At least one was required by invariant.

newState.summary: R6 removes `policy` and `policyRule`, adds optional `regulatoryBasis`, `policyBasis`, and `policyText`, and has no equivalent required invariant.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 separates regulatory codes, computable backing policy reference/URI, and human-readable policy text, but all are optional in the base resource.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances satisfying `ppc-1` by carrying `policy` or `policyRule` contain elements that R6 no longer permits. R6 can also express a Consent with no computable or textual policy basis, which would violate the R4 invariant. The migration is not one-to-one: policyRule, policy URI, regulatory basis, and human policy text have different meanings.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The policy basis is central to determining what rules the consent authorizes or prohibits.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating regulatory basis, computable policy identity, and human-readable policy evidence is a reasonable R6 modeling goal. The R4 fields and invariant were coarse, and old `policyRule` values do not map one-to-one to the new elements. Retaining the old fields would reduce breakage, but it would keep multiple policy representations with unclear precedence. The redesign is probably justified, with the caveat that migration and profile constraints are needed.
justification.inferredGoal: Separate regulatory basis, computable policy identity, and human-readable policy evidence.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain policy and policyRule as deprecated fields while adding regulatoryBasis, policyBasis, and policyText plus profile or best-practice rules for policy presence.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could accept R4 `policy` and `policyRule` while adding `regulatoryBasis`, `policyBasis`, and `policyText`. That is a real base-design alternative, but only partial: processors would need precedence and consistency rules across old and new policy elements, deprecated policy representations might persist, and implementations could still disagree about which policy basis is enforceable.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old data but leaves overlapping policy facts and ambiguous old policyRule semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 has `Consent.policy` 0..*.
R4 has `Consent.policyRule` 0..1 with extensible consent-policy binding.
R4 requires policy or policyRule.
R6 adds optional `regulatoryBasis`.
R6 adds optional `policyBasis` with reference and uri children.
R6 adds optional `policyText`.
No R6 local equivalent of ppc-1 is present.

examples.examplesMd: The `policyRule` to `regulatoryBasis` mapping is illustrative only; some R4 policyRule values may be better represented as `policyBasis.uri` or `policyText`.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 significantly remodels how the backing policy is represented. This is both a structural break and a conformance change: an R4 instance had to point to a policy or policy rule, while R6 base Consent does not require the new policy-related fields.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `policy` and `policyRule` are unknown in R6. R6 instances lacking any policy basis are not R4-valid because R4 required policy or policyRule. Code that assumes a policy basis exists after base validation can no longer rely on that invariant in R6.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Classify each R4 policy artifact: map jurisdictional/regulatory codes to `regulatoryBasis`, computable policy references or URIs to `policyBasis.reference`/`policyBasis.uri`, and human policy documents to `policyText`. Preserve unmappable content in extensions and add profile constraints if your implementation still requires a policy basis.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 split is semantically cleaner but could have been introduced compatibly by retaining old fields and weakening `ppc-1` gradually. Removing the invariant may be appropriate for a base resource, but implementations should consider restoring it in profiles.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Manual review is needed for R4 `policyRule` values because the element mixed computable policy and regulatory examples.

findings.title: Consent.verification.verificationDate was renamed to date and verification metadata was expanded

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 captured at most one verification timestamp and had no explicit verifier or verification type element.

newState.summary: R6 date is 0..* dateTime; R6 also adds verification.type and verification.verifiedBy, and widens verifiedWith to include Group.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 supports a history of verification dates, a business type for verification, the actor who performed verification, and group verification-with targets.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements have the same definition role: when consent was verified. The R6 path is shorter and repeatable.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `verificationDate` fail R6 validation unless renamed to `verification.date`. R6 can carry multiple dates and verifier/type metadata that R4 cannot represent in base fields. Runtime risk is medium because verification is optional, but systems that rely on it for legal evidence need careful migration.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting repeated verification or re-validation events and richer verification metadata is reasonable. The specific rename of `verificationDate` to `date` was avoidable: the old optional element could have been retained for compatibility while new repeatable dates, type, and verifiedBy were added. The duplicate-date tradeoff is manageable compared with invalidating existing verification data.
justification.inferredGoal: Support repeated verification/re-validation events with richer metadata.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain verificationDate as a deprecated singleton while adding repeatable date and richer verification metadata.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `Consent.verification.verificationDate` as `0..1` and add `Consent.verification.date` for additional or structured verification dates, with an invariant or guidance that both fields not disagree. This preserves R4 instances and still supports the R6 history use case. The risk is that deprecated and new date representations may both be populated unless profiles or validators constrain them.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Duplicate verification-date fields need consistency rules but the tradeoff is moderate and preserves old verification records.

evidence.detail: R4 has verificationDate 0..1 dateTime.
R6 has date 0..* dateTime.
R6 adds verification.type.
R6 adds verification.verifiedBy.
R6 adds Group as a verifiedWith target.

findings.narrativeMd: The verification backbone keeps its required `verified` boolean, but the date element is renamed and made repeatable, and R6 adds verifier metadata. This affects legal/audit workflows more than everyday consent records.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `verificationDate` is unknown in R6. R6 multiple `date` values, `type`, `verifiedBy`, and Group `verifiedWith` cannot be represented in base R4 without loss or extensions. Generated code must update property names and cardinalities.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `verificationDate` to `date` and wrap the value as a list if your R6 model represents repeatables as arrays. For downgrade, keep only one date or preserve extra dates in extensions/audit records. Validate that the required `verification.verified` remains present for every verification item.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The richer R6 verification model is likely justified, but the simple date rename could have been handled as a compatibility alias or deprecation.

findings.title: Provision permit/deny semantics moved from provision.type to root modifier Consent.decision, and provision became repeatable

oldState.summary: R4 `provision.type` was an optional required-bound code on each provision; root provision max was 1.

semanticText.definition: Action to take - permit or deny - when the rule conditions are met. Not permitted in root rule, required in all nested rules.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 encoded permit/deny on `provision.type`; nested provision semantics could explicitly state permit or deny.

newState.summary: R6 removes `provision.type`, adds root `Consent.decision` as a modifier, and changes `Consent.provision` max from 1 to *.

flags.isModifierReason: Sets context for the values in .provision

semanticText.definition: Action to take - permit or deny - as default.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 sets a base decision and says provisions are assumed to negate the previous level.

facts.note: Code values are stable, but their structural location and semantics changed.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Both elements use the consent-provision-type ValueSet (`deny`/`permit`), but R6 moves the value to a root default decision and changes nested provision interpretation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances with `provision.type` are invalid in R6, and the semantics are not a simple field move for nested provisions. R6 `decision` is a new modifier element; processors that ignore it can invert the meaning of provisions. R6 multiple root provisions are not representable in R4, where the root provision max was 1.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Permit/deny inversion is a direct access-control risk.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of making the base permit/deny decision explicit and treating provisions as exceptions is reasonable and safety-relevant. A less-breaking design could retain `provision.type`, but dual explicit and inferred permit/deny semantics would be hard for evaluators to reconcile and could invert access decisions. Because the compatibility alternative has material safety tradeoffs, the breaking modifier redesign is probably justified, provided migration rules are explicit.
justification.inferredGoal: Clarify a base permit/deny decision and model provisions as exceptions or negations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add root decision while retaining provision.type for explicit legacy or nested decisions with strict reconciliation rules.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Retaining `provision.type` would be a base-design alternative that lets R4 provisions validate while new instances use root `decision`. It is only partial because evaluators would need precedence rules between root `decision`, inferred negation, and explicit nested `provision.type`; if any processor ignored one representation, permit/deny semantics could be reversed. Deprecated decision representations could also accumulate indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances but creates dangerous dual permit/deny semantics and conflict risk in access-control evaluation.

evidence.detail: R4 has provision.type 0..1 required-bound to deny/permit.
R6 adds Consent.decision 0..1, required-bound to deny/permit, isModifier true.
R6 changes Consent.provision max to *.
Both R4 and R6 code systems contain deny and permit.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example only covers a simple root provision. Nested R4 provisions with explicit `type` values may require custom logic.

findings.narrativeMd: This is a high-risk semantic change because it affects permit/deny evaluation. R6 introduces a modifier `decision`; applications must understand it before interpreting provisions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `provision.type` is not valid in R6. R6 `decision` is not valid in R4 and is a modifier, so ignoring it is unsafe. R6 repeatable root provisions cannot downgrade to the R4 `0..1` root provision without merging or loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Build explicit tests for opt-in, opt-out, nested exception, and multiple-root-provision scenarios. Map simple R4 root `provision.type` to `decision` only after confirming the R4 instance used root type that way. For nested rules, document and test how explicit R4 permit/deny maps to R6 negation semantics.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Moving a decision to a root modifier may be cleaner for R6 evaluators, but retaining `provision.type` as a deprecated explicit override would have reduced migration ambiguity.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding needs domain review because access-control semantics can be inverted by an incorrect transform.

findings.title: Provision actor role and reference changed from mandatory to optional, and role binding changed

oldState.summary: In each actor, role and reference were both 1..1; role was extensible-bound to security-role-type.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 actor entries had to identify both how the actor was involved and the actor resource.

newState.summary: In each actor, role and reference are both 0..1; role is extensible-bound to participation-role-type.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 allows actor entries with only a role, only a reference, or neither structurally, subject to profiles or business rules.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This does not make R4 instances invalid in R6 because the requirements were weakened. The risk is downgrade and runtime assumptions: R6 actor rows may be incomplete for R4, and role terminology changed from a broad security-role-type set to an R6 participation-role-type set.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Changing `role` and `reference` from mandatory to optional does not make R4-valid actor entries invalid in R6. The binding change is also extensible rather than a strict required-code removal. The goal of allowing role-only or reference-only actor descriptions is plausible, and stricter implementations can restore requirements in profiles. This is not a forward R4-to-R6 base-design break.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow provisions to describe actors by role or reference independently and align role binding with participation terminology.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 backward-compatible alternative is needed because R6 weakens the actor child cardinalities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: An invariant requiring at least one of `role` or `reference` may be a good data-quality improvement, but it is not a backward-compatible alternative to an R4-to-R6 break. It would constrain new R6 content for cleaner downgrade and safer processing rather than preserve old R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The issue is R6-to-R4 downgrade and data-quality risk for incomplete R6 actors, not preservation of R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 role min is 1.
R4 reference min is 1.
R6 role min is 0 and ValueSet is participation-role-type.
R6 reference min is 0.
R6 binding uses participation-role-type instead of R4 security-role-type; local compose definitions differ.

examples.examplesMd: The example is valid against the R6 base cardinalities but cannot satisfy R4 actor.reference 1..1.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 weakens actor child requirements. That gives more modeling flexibility but means base R6 validation no longer guarantees each actor has both a role and a concrete reference.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is not a validation break. R6-to-R4 fails when an actor lacks role or reference. Code written against R4 may dereference actor.role and actor.reference without null checks, so R6 content can produce runtime errors or incomplete enforcement decisions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When downgrading, reject actor entries missing role or reference unless a local extension can preserve the missing concept. For R6 processing, add null-safe handling and profile constraints if your consent engine requires fully specified actors.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Optional children are backward compatible in the forward direction but reduce guarantees. An invariant requiring at least one child would have preserved most flexibility with better data quality.

findings.title: Consent.provision.class was split into documentType and resourceType with changed bindings

oldState.summary: R4 provision.class was 0..* Coding with extensible ConsentContentClass binding covering resource types, profiles, CDA, and other classes.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 used one `class` element for resource type, profile, CDA, and other content classes.

newState.summary: R6 removes class and adds documentType 0..* Coding preferred-bound to consent-content-class and resourceType 0..* Coding extensible-bound to resource-types.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires migration logic to decide whether an old class code identifies a document type or a FHIR resource/profile type.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 `documentType` and `resourceType` definitions split the combined R4 `class` definition into document and resource/profile cases.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `provision.class` are R6-invalid because the element was removed. Transforming the data requires classification of each code, and some R4 codes may not clearly belong in documentType or resourceType. R6 resourceType codes and documentType split cannot be represented losslessly in R4 without collapsing them back into class.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misclassifying covered data classes can over-share or under-share protected content.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating document-type constraints from FHIR resource/profile constraints is a reasonable interoperability goal. The old `class` bucket cannot express that distinction without code interpretation, and some old codings may be ambiguous. Keeping `class` would reduce validation failures but prolong the ambiguity the split addresses. The break is therefore probably justified, although it needs ConceptMap-style guidance.
justification.inferredGoal: Separate document-type constraints from FHIR resource/profile-type constraints.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep broad class as deprecated while adding documentType and resourceType with precedence and mapping guidance.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have accepted deprecated `Consent.provision.class` while adding `documentType` and `resourceType`. That would preserve R4 instances, but processors would need to reconcile broad class codings with the split fields, route uncertain codings, and avoid conflicting content-targeting declarations. The old broad bucket could also persist indefinitely, so the alternative is only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old instances but keeps ambiguous content-class semantics and requires merging three targeting axes.

evidence.detail: R4 `class` covers FHIR resource type, profile, CDA, or other type.
R6 `documentType` covers document types.
R6 `resourceType` covers FHIR resource types or profiles.
R4 consent-content-class includes formatcodes and resource-types; R6 consent-content-class uses doc-typecodes and examples, while resourceType separately binds to resource-types.

examples.examplesMd: The example assumes a resource-type code; CDA or MIME-like codes should instead be evaluated for `documentType`.

findings.narrativeMd: `provision.class` was a broad bucket. R6 makes the targeting axis more explicit, but existing data must be inspected to route each code to the correct new element.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `provision.class` is unknown in R6. R6 `documentType` and `resourceType` are unknown in R4. Binding changes also affect validation expectations: R6 `resourceType` uses a resource-types ValueSet, while `documentType` is only preferred-bound to consent-content-class.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Classify old `class` codings by system and value. Resource type/profile codes should map to `resourceType`; document/template/MIME/CDA codes should map to `documentType`. Preserve uncertain codings and require human review before using them for enforcement.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The split could have been introduced as additive fields while keeping `class` deprecated. That would have reduced breakage but left ambiguous targeting semantics in place.

findings.title: Provision securityLabel binding weakened from extensible security-labels to example security-label-example

oldState.summary: Extensible binding to the broad security-labels ValueSet.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 validators could require use of the security-labels set when an applicable code existed.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 treats the referenced security labels as examples rather than an extensible conformance set.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This does not invalidate R4 instances in R6; the binding is weaker. The risk is semantic and policy-level: R6 base validation provides less terminology pressure for interoperable security labels, so applications relying on base conformance for access-control labels may see more local codes.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Security labels influence privacy and access-control decisions.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The binding weakening is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break. The inferred goal of avoiding over-constrained security-label terminology in the base resource is plausible, even though security labels are important for access control. Implementations needing stronger terminology guarantees should use profiles, but backward-compatible alternative availability is not applicable.
justification.inferredGoal: Avoid over-constraining security-label terminology in the base Consent resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not a backward-compatible-alternative case; weakening the binding does not invalidate R4 securityLabel codings.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping the R4 extensible binding could be a stronger conformance choice, but it is not needed to preserve R4 instances because the R6 example binding is already more permissive. The relevant design question is interoperability and safety policy, not backward compatibility of the base wire format.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is lower base interoperability pressure versus jurisdictional flexibility, not R4 instance preservation.

evidence.detail: R4 binding strength is extensible to security-labels.
R6 binding strength is example to security-label-example.
The R4 ValueSet composes HL7 v3 security label value sets; R6 uses example data/event label sets.

examples.examplesMd: No specific instance becomes invalid because of this weakening. The issue is downstream interoperability and policy interpretation.

findings.narrativeMd: Security labels remain structurally the same, but base terminology conformance becomes weaker. This can be beneficial for flexibility but risky for systems expecting standard labels to drive consent enforcement.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is not broken; if anything, R6 accepts more local terminology. The compatibility issue is behavioral: two R6 systems may exchange security-label codings that pass base validation but are not mutually understood.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not rely on base R6 binding strength for security-label interoperability. Define profile bindings or policy-specific allowed code systems for production access-control flows, and test unknown/local security labels explicitly.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The weakening is backward-compatible for instances but less strict. A stronger base binding plus profile-level escape hatches would preserve interoperability but might overconstrain jurisdictions.

findings.title: R6 adds local Consent fields with no base R4 representation, including provision.expression and policy/verification/controller fields

oldState.summary: R4 has no base elements for R6 `provision.expression`, `controller`, `manager`, `policyText`, `policyBasis`, `regulatoryBasis`, `verification.type`, or `verification.verifiedBy`.
oldState.narrativeMd: Some concepts can be approximated by R4 fields, but several R6 additions have no direct base R4 slot.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional fields for computable provision expressions, management/enforcement actors, policy evidence, regulatory basis, and richer verification metadata.
newState.narrativeMd: The most conversion-sensitive addition is `Consent.provision.expression`, an `Expression` that can define what is controlled by a consent in a computable way.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These optional additions do not break R4-to-R6 validation, but R6 instances that use them cannot be downgraded to base R4 without loss, extensions, or external records. `provision.expression` is especially important because it may carry executable consent scope logic.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Dropping computable consent expressions or enforcement actors can change access decisions.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: These fields add new optional R6 expressivity and do not invalidate old R4 instances. The downgrade risk is real, especially for computable provision expressions and controller/manager roles, but that is not a backward-compatible base-design problem. The appropriate calibration is therefore `Not applicable`, not `No` based on extension or backport mitigations.
justification.inferredGoal: Add missing consent workflow, policy evidence, and computable-expression capabilities.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Optional additive R6 fields are forward-compatible; no less-breaking base R6 alternative is needed for R4-to-R6.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: There is no forward-compatibility alternative to assess: avoiding the optional additions would reduce R6 expressivity rather than preserve R4 data. R4 clients may need cross-version extensions, sidecar policy artifacts, or R4-compatible profiles for downgrade, but those are mitigation strategies and not backwards-compatible R6 base designs.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The cost is R6-to-R4 downgrade loss, handled by profiles, extensions, or conversion policy rather than a different R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R6 adds provision.expression 0..1 Expression.
R6 adds controller 0..* Reference.
R6 adds policyText 0..* Reference(DocumentReference).
R6 adds verifiedBy 0..1 Reference.

examples.examplesMd: The expression example is illustrative; actual R6 Expression content must follow implementation policy and profiles.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional capabilities that should not be dismissed just because they are not R4-to-R6 breaking. They become important when trying to serve R6 data to R4 clients or maintain a common persistence model.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validators reject these R6 elements. Lossless downgrade requires extensions, separate policy resources, or rejecting such instances. Code generators and databases need new nullable/repeating fields.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For dual-version systems, define a downgrade policy: either prohibit these R6 fields in R4-compatible profiles, map them to cross-version extensions, or maintain them in a sidecar store. Pay special attention to `provision.expression` because omitting it can make a consent appear broader or narrower than intended.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The additions are forward-compatible by design. The main issue is not avoidability, but the need to document downgrade limitations and avoid silent data loss.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, baseDefinition, derivation, and abstract flag are unchanged. Status/maturity changed but not as an identity break.
No local Consent fixed value, pattern, or defaultValue constraints were found as material R4-to-R6 changes.
No local slicing definitions were identified on Consent elements in either StructureDefinition.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraints were found as material changes.
`consent-provision-type` and `consent-data-meaning` required code sets have the same codes in the inspected local CodeSystems, even though versions/displays/status changed.
`Consent.sourceReference` target resources and `Consent.provision.data.reference` target Resource remain materially the same; other Consent reference target changes are covered in findings.
No new local Consent invariants were found in R6. Removed local R4 `ppc-*` invariants are covered in findings. Inherited `dom-*` constraint expression changes are out of scope.
`Consent.status` remains a modifier. The local removal of modifier `scope` and addition of modifier `decision` are covered in findings; inherited modifierExtension behavior is out of scope.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Consent standards status changed from trial-use/draft to normative/active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The artifact retains the same canonical identity, kind, type, baseDefinition, and abstract flag. Maturity/status changes do not by themselves invalidate instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The normative status may raise expectations for stability and conformance, but the R6 ballot content still has many model changes from R4.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Consent.category became optional and example-bound
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This is not R4-to-R6 instance-breaking because it lowers cardinality from 1 to 0 and weakens the binding from extensible to example.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: R6 instances with no category are not R4-representable without adding a category, and systems that relied on base category presence should add profile constraints.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds root Consent.period for effective period
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element is optional, so existing R4 instances do not become invalid solely because it exists in R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: R6-to-R4 downgrade may need an extension or a policy for folding root period into provisions or external metadata.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Consent-related CodeSystems changed status/version
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Version and publication status changes are not instance-breaking when codes are unchanged, as with consent-provision-type and consent-data-meaning.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Use version-aware terminology validation, especially for required bindings where codes did change, such as Consent.status.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited changes to `language`, contained-resource constraints, narrative conditions, and base extension behavior were intentionally excluded and should be handled by base-artifact reports.

The package indexes show search parameter changes aligned with the model changes, including R6 subject/grantor/grantee/manager/controller/verified additions and R4 scope/organization/consentor removals. These are out of scope for the resource StructureDefinition report but important for API migration.
A formal ConceptMap is needed for `proposed` and `rejected` migration and for R6 `not-done`/`unknown` downgrade handling.
Terminology-server expansions would improve confidence for category, securityLabel, participation-role-type, resource-types, and external terminology systems not fully packaged locally.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 diff or ballot change proposal was available in the local package inputs. Justification and backward-compatible alternative assessments are therefore inferred from StructureDefinitions.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review HL7 ballot change notes, Jira tickets, and official comparison pages for Consent.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official cross-version ConceptMaps were found for Consent element mappings or R4-to-R6 Consent status codes. Ambiguous mappings are flagged for human review.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Publish or inspect official cross-version maps for Consent and ConsentState.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology analysis used local CodeSystem and ValueSet compose definitions rather than server-side expansions. External systems such as HL7 terminology, LOINC, DICOM, and v3 value sets may have additional changes.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run expansions for R4 and R6 ValueSets in a terminology server configured with matching package versions.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The report does not assess profiles, implementation guides, or jurisdictional policy rules that may restore requirements such as policy basis, category, subject type, or actor completeness.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Analyze relevant IG profiles and local conformance artifacts.

crossArtifactPatternsToCheck: modifier element additions for workflow decision semantics
